Assuming the body has enough glucose and other sources of energy, those amino acids will 
be used in one of the following ways: 
332
TAMBERLY POWELL, MS, RDN

• Protein synthesis in cells around the body 
• Making nonessential amino acids needed for protein synthesis 
• Making other nitrogen-containing compounds 
• Rearranged and stored as fat (there is no storage form of protein) 
• Small amount metabolized as fuel, for an immediate source of ATP 
If there is not enough glucose or energy available, amino acids can also be used in one of these 
ways: 
• Rearranged into glucose for fuel for the brain and red blood cells 
• Greater amount metabolized as fuel, for an immediate source of ATP 
In order to use amino acids to make ATP, glucose, or fat, the nitrogen first has to be removed 
in a process called deamination, which occurs in the liver and kidneys. The nitrogen is initially 
released as ammonia, and because ammonia is toxic, the liver transforms it into urea. Urea is then 
transported to the kidneys and excreted in the urine. Urea is a molecule that contains two nitrogens 
and is highly soluble in water. This makes it ideal for transporting excess nitrogen out of the body. 
Because amino acids are building blocks that the body reserves in order to synthesize other 
proteins, more than 90 percent of the protein ingested does not get broken down further than the 
amino acid monomers.
